canonicalExplanation.summary: `git bisect` finds **the first commit where something broke** by **binary search**. You mark one commit **good** (worked) and one **bad** (broken). Git checks out the midpoint; you test and mark it; Git halves the range again. With 1,000 commits, that's about **10 tests**. It only works with a **reliable test**: the same commit must always give the same answer. Automate it with `git bisect run ./test.sh` (exit 0 = good, 125 = skip, most other codes from 1 to 127 = bad). Bisect finds a **commit**, not a culprit person. Read that commit's patch to confirm the cause, then `git bisect reset`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
The export button worked in release v1.0. It's broken on today's main, 200 commits later. A learner starts reading every commit message, and after an hour they've found nothing. A deterministic regression script marks release v1 good and current main bad, then classifies midpoint commits until one introducing commit remains. In this lesson you'll locate a seeded regression with bisect and verify the causative patch.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Dependencies and reproducible builds**, **Commits and history**, **Log, show and graph** and **Build and task commands**.

sections.heading: The model: binary search over history
sections.body:
```bash
# test-export.sh: exit 0 if export works, 1 if broken, 125 to skip.
npm ci --silent && npm run build --silent || exit 125
node scripts/check-export.js
```

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad main              # broken here.
git bisect good v1.0             # worked here.
git bisect run ./test-export.sh  # Git tests midpoints automatically.
# ... 8 steps later:
# 4c1e2f9 is the first bad commit.
git show 4c1e2f9                 # read the patch: confirm the cause.
git bisect reset                 # return to where you started.
```

| Exit code | Bisect reads it as |
|---|---|
| 0. | good. |
| other codes from 1 to 127. | bad. |
| 125. | skip: this commit can't be tested. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why exit 125 when the build fails?", "answer": "A commit that doesn't build can't tell you whether export works. Skipping it avoids wrongly marking it bad and sending bisect in the wrong direction."}
```

examples.title: Finding the regression since v1
examples.situation: A deterministic regression script marks release v1 good and current main bad, then classifies midpoint commits until one introducing commit remains.
walkthrough: **A deterministic regression script:** test-export.sh builds and checks export, and skips unbuildable commits.
**Marks release v1 good and current main bad:** git bisect good v1.0; git bisect bad main.
**Classifies midpoint commits until one introducing commit remains:** after 8 runs, 4c1e2f9; git show will reveal a renamed CSV field.
examples.result: The regression is found in minutes, and the patch confirms the cause.

examples.title: The flaky bisect
examples.situation: Bisect points at a commit that only changed the README. The learner's test depends on network timing.
walkthrough: A README change can't break export; the result is suspect.
The test is flaky, so one midpoint was mis-marked.
Replace the network call with a local fixture, then bisect again.
examples.result: The second bisect lands on a commit that really changed export code.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Bisect examines code changes automatically and determines which developer caused a bug without a reproducible test.
misconceptions.correction: Bisect only checks out commits; your test decides good or bad. It needs a reliable test, finds a commit rather than a person, and you must confirm the cause by reading the patch.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The flaky bisect", why did bisect blame a README change?

analogy.example: Bisect is like **finding a burnt-out bulb in a long string of fairy lights** by testing the middle, then the middle of the bad half, and so on. It only works if your tester is reliable. A tester that flickers sends you to the wrong half.
limitations: Bulbs don't depend on each other; some commits won't build (skip them).
Finding the bulb isn't blaming whoever hung the lights.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a sandbox repo with 20 commits, seed a bug in one of them. Find it with manual git bisect good/bad, then again with bisect run and a script, and confirm with git show.
scaffold: Make a script that exits 0 or 1.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a bisect test script for a real regression in one of your projects, including exit 125 for commits that don't build. Run it, confirm the introducing patch, and write a short incident note with the commit, cause and fix.
scaffold: Test the script on known good and bad commits first.
Always git bisect reset at the end.

remediation.explanation: Before bisecting, prove your test: **run it on the known good and bad commits, twice each.** Same answers? Then bisect.

recap.summary: To locate a regression with bisect, write a deterministic good/bad test, mark a known good and a known bad commit, let git bisect (or bisect run) halve the range, skip untestable commits with exit 125, then read the first bad commit's patch to confirm the cause and run git bisect reset.
